summary:
North Carolina lies within the United States, and the federal layer governs the sharpest exposures a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, a restriction that reaches federal buildings in North Carolina. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves passports already issued with an X marker valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect.

Facilities access in North Carolina has been the state's defining trans issue since 2016. After the Charlotte city council passed an ordinance in March 2016 allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, the North Carolina General Assembly met in emergency session and passed House Bill 2, which required people to use public bathrooms corresponding with the sex listed on their birth certificate and barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people. The law drew global backlash, with companies including Google and Disney pledging to pull back business, and the U.S. Justice Department called it state-sponsored discrimination and sued, prompting North Carolina to file its own suit. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017.

Facility-use policy remains unsettled. WRAL reported on 25 March 2025 that Republican lawmakers were again pushing a bathroom bill in that year's session, years after the HB 2 boycotts, so a visitor to North Carolina should treat restroom and changing-room access as contingent on the status of pending legislation and on the rules of the specific venue rather than as a settled right.

North Carolina carries a documented lethal-violence exposure. An investigative data analysis published by The Needle on 16 July 2026, comparing legal-risk tiers with Trans Murder Monitoring records, places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women with three or more recorded victims and characterises the state as moderate-risk; the analysis notes the victim count is an acknowledged undercount and argues that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women.
tangentialFactors:
North Carolina sits in the middle of a national pattern rather than at its edge. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban; some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances, and in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's law.

The same Needle analysis that rates North Carolina moderate-risk finds that higher legal-protection tiers do not reliably translate into lower homicide rates for trans women, so the absence of a standing state facility ban in North Carolina should not be read as evidence of physical safety.

North Carolina's trajectory diverges from states that have hardened their rules in 2026: Kansas enacted a law in February 2026 preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and a July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the fourth state placed on a "Do Not Travel" list for trans people. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and facility restrictions are expanding in multiple legislatures during the 2026 session.

The federal travel environment applies equally inside North Carolina. Multiple foreign governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States in 2025 over identity-document and data rules, at least eight European countries adjusted entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, and TSA screening procedures can involve secondary screening and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy.
localsOnly:
North Carolina's residents live with the afterlife of House Bill 2 as a political cycle rather than a closed chapter: the 2016 ordinance, the emergency-session response, the corporate and federal backlash, and the March 2017 repeal are the reference points every subsequent facility dispute is argued against.

Because HB 2 barred municipalities from adopting their own anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people, local protections in North Carolina depend on what the General Assembly permits; residents seeking recourse for discrimination may find no local ordinance to invoke.

Facility-use rules for schools, state buildings and other public venues are subject to change within the legislative session, so residents face a policy environment that can shift between sessions rather than a fixed statutory position.

Residents who changed identity documents in earlier years do so under federal record rules now governed by Executive Order 14168 and the State Department's processing decisions, which affect name and gender changes on passports held by North Carolinians as well as visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the bathroom bill advanced by North Carolina Republicans in the 2025 session was enacted, vetoed or left pending is not established by the available sources; the inventory supports only that it was being pushed in that session.

The precise scope of facility rules currently in force in North Carolina after the 30 March 2017 repeal of House Bill 2 is unresolved here. The sources establish that HB 2's birth-certificate-sex bathroom requirement existed and was repealed, but do not describe what replaced it, whether any narrower restriction survives, or how the repeal interacts with Executive Order 14168 in federally funded settings.

The North Carolina homicide figure of 3.0 killings per 100,000 trans women derives from a source that itself labels the victim count an undercount, and the underlying methodology for assigning a risk tier is not verifiable from this inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses North Carolina-specific rules on birth-certificate or driver's-licence gender markers, state hate-crime coverage of anti-trans offences, state recognition of partner or marital status, or any state-level restriction on gender-affirming care. Those questions remain not sourced rather than confirmed absent.
